description:
## Where we are

`mean_flow_stages` takes four numbers per rotor row as free inputs: lift coefficient, drag coefficient, solidity, and blade velocity coefficient. Only solidity is geometry. The other three are hand-set, so a stage's performance is currently asserted by the caller rather than derived from a blade.

The exit flow angle is also taken as the blade metal angle exactly. Real cascades deviate from their metal angle, and nothing here models that.

## The trap, written down before anyone falls into it

The obvious way to get a lift coefficient is the classical cascade relation:

```text
C_L = 2 (s/c) cos(beta_m) (tan beta1 - tan beta2) - C_D tan(beta_m)
```

**Do not use it here.** It is algebraically equivalent to the Euler work: substituting it into the reaction term reproduces `U (c_theta1 - c_theta2)` exactly. There is already a test asserting that identity (`lift_route_agrees_with_momentum_route_at_the_cascade_lift_coefficient` in the pre-split test set, now covered by the two-mechanism tests). Since this model takes the impulse part from the Euler equation *and then adds* a reaction part, deriving `C_L` from flow turning would count the same momentum twice.

Geometry-derived lift has to come from a route that is **independent of the flow turning**: incidence and camber, not `tan beta1 - tan beta2`.

## Proposed sequence

Three steps, each independently useful and each testable on its own.

### 1. Exit angle from the throat, not from the metal angle

The strongest and cheapest geometry link. For a converging blade passage the exit flow angle follows the throat opening and pitch:

```text
beta2 ~ arccos(o / s)
```

with `o` the throat opening. This replaces "exit angle is whatever the caller typed" with "exit angle is what the passage geometry allows", and it feeds straight into the existing velocity triangle with no change to the work mechanisms. Deviation correlations refine it at low Mach; the cosine rule is the base case.

### 2. Lift coefficient from incidence and camber

Blade geometry gives an inlet metal angle, a camber angle, a stagger angle and a chord. The relative inlet angle comes from the triangle. Incidence is the difference. Thin-aerofoil theory then gives a lift-curve slope about the zero-lift line, corrected for cascade effects by the usual interference factor.

This is independent of `tan beta1 - tan beta2`, which is what keeps it clear of the trap above.

### 3. Losses from a cascade correlation

Replace the hand-set drag coefficient and blade velocity coefficient with a standard turbine cascade loss system. Ainley-Mathieson with the Dunham-Came and Kacker-Okapuu updates is the usual choice for steam and gas turbine rows, giving profile, secondary and tip-clearance loss from geometry plus Reynolds and Mach corrections.

This is the step that would let a stage efficiency be *predicted* rather than supplied, which is the point of the whole exercise.

## What a `BladeGeometry` type would carry

Chord, pitch, throat opening, inlet and exit metal angles, camber, stagger, maximum thickness and its position, leading and trailing edge radii, blade height, and tip clearance. Solidity becomes derived rather than given.

## Acceptance

- A stage built from blade geometry alone, with no performance coefficients supplied, produces a sensible efficiency and turning.
- The double-counting trap is guarded by a test, not just by this note: assert that the geometry-derived lift coefficient is **not** the cascade-relation value for a case where the two differ.
- Existing hand-set coefficients still work, so this is additive rather than a replacement.

## Related

Follow-up to the mean-flow stage model. Same crate, same module.
title: tampines-steam-tables: derive blade coefficients from geometry, not from hand-set inputs

description: Follow-up split from op-e46.4 (DelayedNeutronLayer O(1) fix, done). teh-o-prke nordheim_fuchs::advance_with_reactivity_driver takes a &mut TransferFnFirstOrder and calls set_user_input_and_calc every step; if driven in an always-on real-time loop with a changing commanded reactivity it accumulates one FirstOrderResponse per input change (pruned only after 20*tau), i.e. the same O(n)/step + unbounded-memory growth op-e46.4 fixed in the delayed layer. NOT currently triggered in the shipped fhr_sim_v2 (prke_backend uses nordheim_fuchs.set_external_reactivity(...) directly, no TransferFn), so latent, not live. Options mirror op-e46.4: give the caller an O(1) exponential/implicit-integrator reactivity-lag path instead of a growing TransferFnFirstOrder, or periodically rebase the lag. Reference op-e46.4 / op-dt3.11.

notes.author: teddy0@arch-aftershock-rapid-glass-S267454
notes.content:
LIKELY RESOLVED BY op-fm5's fix (2026-08-11) -- maintainer to confirm and close.

The mechanism this bead describes no longer exists. As of chem-eng 0.2.0, TransferFnFirstOrder does not accumulate a FirstOrderResponse per input change: both of its constituent blocks (FirstOrderStableTransferFnNoZeroes and FirstOrderStableTransferFnForZeroes) now advance by an exact O(1) zero-order-hold recurrence carrying 2 and 1 state variables respectively, with no Vec and no 20*tau pruning. So nordheim_fuchs::advance_with_reactivity_driver can be driven in an always-on real-time loop at any timestep without the O(n)/step growth or unbounded memory.

Measured: filtered PID at dt=0.001 s with tau_d=80.8 s -- exactly the PRKE shape this bead worried about -- went from 2329.52 us/step and still rising at step 79,000, to a flat 0.17 us/step. Guarded by block_state_size_does_not_grow_with_step_index and pid_step_cost_does_not_grow_with_step_index in chem-eng.

No change was needed in teh-o-prke itself. Neither of the two remedies this bead proposed (an O(1) reactivity-lag path, or periodic rebasing) is required any more.

title: NF reactivity driver: same TransferFnFirstOrder response_vec growth in per-step loops

description: add_boundary_layers is V&V'd + reliable on FLAT (box) walls but invalidates the mesh on CURVED walls (snapped sphere/cylinder) and on polygonal (dual) wall faces — the averaged inward-normal extrusion self-intersects / inverts on convex curvature. Mesh Studio currently gracefully SKIPS layers there (falls back to the valid polyhedral dual) and reports it. Needed for real curved-geometry CFD near-wall resolution: per-point feature-aware normals, layer-thickness limiting by local cell size, layer collapse/termination where cells would invert (snappyHexMesh addLayers strategy). V&V: sphere/cylinder + N layers -> valid + solvable, prism cells present at the wall, volume conserved. Blocks the full 'polyhedral mesh with layers' story for curved reactors in Mesh Studio (examples/mesh_studio).

notes.author: root@vm
notes.content: Curved-wall layers working (commit a52636a): add_boundary_layers_adaptive — smoothed normal field (Laplacian passes over wall-point adjacency) + per-point thickness cap (fraction of local wall spacing) + global validity back-off (scale down until closed). Diagnosis: min-faces dual + THIN layers was already valid on the sphere; failure was thickness-driven self-intersection, not topology — back-off targets that. Mesh Studio now inserts real prism layers on sphere (6583 cells) + cylinder (3978), valid, 0 inverted, volume conserved. BL non-orthogonality ~79-81deg is expected (>checkMesh 70deg warning, handled by non-orthogonal correctors) — GUI explains this. V&V: 3 tests (sphere/cylinder/box). REMAINING (keep open): back-off is GLOBAL (one tight feature thins whole wall); true per-point LOCAL layer termination + height-by-feature-size (snappyHexMesh addLayers / AFLR advancing-layer) still to do for optimal thickness on mixed-curvature geometry.

title: cfmesh: boundary layers on curved / polyhedral walls (snappyHexMesh-style layer addition)
